Chara
khah-RAH
noun
Greek chara, joy; closely kin to charis, grace; the gladness of heart that is the fruit of the Spirit.

Biblical Definition

Chara is the Greek word for joy, the gladness of heart that is a fruit of the Spirit and a mark of the kingdom of God, which is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. It is closely kin to charis, grace, for the joy of the believer springs from the grace of God: joy is grace received and rejoiced in. This joy is not the fleeting mirth of the world, which depends on outward circumstance, but a deep and abiding gladness rooted in God and His salvation, which can fill the heart even in tribulation. The Lord told His disciples these things He spoke that His joy might remain in them, and that their joy might be full; the apostles, beaten, departed rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name; Paul, in prison, bids the Philippians Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. The believer is to count it all joy when he falls into divers temptations, and looks unto Jesus, who for the joy that was set before Him endured the cross. The full and final chara is the entering into the joy of the Lord. The dictionary honors chara as the Spirit-given joy of the Christian—not dependent on circumstance but rooted in grace, surviving and even triumphing in suffering, the foretaste of the everlasting gladness of the redeemed in the presence of their Lord, in whose presence is fulness of joy.

Key Scripture

Gal 5:22 — "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,"

Joh 15:11 — "These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full."

Php 4:4 — "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice."

Mat 25:21 — "His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord."

Modern Corruption

Joy is reduced to circumstantial happiness or a duty to perform; Scripture knows chara as Spirit-given gladness rooted in grace, abiding even in affliction.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the word joy. The first reduces it to circumstantial happiness—a passing mood that rises and falls with fortune, indistinguishable from the world’s mirth. The second makes it a mere duty to be performed, a forced cheerfulness pasted over an empty heart. Both miss the nature of chara, which is a fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22), grown by God in the soul, not manufactured by man.

The principle to recover is that biblical joy is Spirit-given gladness rooted in the grace of God, which abides and even triumphs in affliction. It is kin to grace itself; the believer’s joy springs from grace received and rejoiced in. The Lord spoke that His joy might remain in His people, and their joy be full (John 15:11); Paul, in prison, could yet command, Rejoice in the Lord alway (Phil 4:4), for this joy does not depend on circumstance but on the Lord. It is no shallow happiness but the deep gladness that counts trials all joy and looks to the everlasting joy beyond—the entering into the joy of the Lord (Matt 25:21). This is the chara the Spirit gives, a foretaste of the fulness of joy in His presence.
